source.title: Methodological approaches in video analysis studies of hamstring injuries in football: a systematic review

paper.citation: Pellegrini A., Della Villa F., Zago M. Methodological approaches in video analysis studies of hamstring injuries in football: a systematic review. Science and Medicine in Football. 2026;:1-22. doi:10.1080/24733938.2026.2691453.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: What methodological approaches have been used in video-analysis studies of hamstring injuries in football, and how consistent and methodologically robust are those approaches? The review included 11 studies published from 2021 to 2024 involving professional association-football (soccer) players. Individual studies analyzed between 8 and 61 injury videos, and only one included female players. This was a systematic review. Two reviewers independently selected studies and extracted data, with a third reviewer available to resolve disagreements.
paper.tldr: Eleven studies met inclusion criteria; they focused on professional soccer, included 8–61 injury videos per study, and only one study included female players. Only two studies assessed inter- or intra-rater reliability. Video review can support structured description and hypothesis generation after a hamstring injury, but it should not be treated as a stand-alone causal test.
paper.methods: This was a systematic review. Two reviewers independently selected studies and extracted data, with a third reviewer available to resolve disagreements. Extraction focused on injury mechanism, inciting activity, biomechanics, and injury circumstances. Risk of bias and reporting quality were assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools and the QA-SIVAS instrument. Because of substantial methodological heterogeneity, the authors used descriptive narrative synthesis rather than meta-analysis.
paper.findings: Eleven studies met inclusion criteria; they focused on professional soccer, included 8–61 injury videos per study, and only one study included female players. Only two studies assessed inter- or intra-rater reliability. Injury diagnosis was confirmed by MRI in three studies and clinical examination in one, while other studies relied on medical records or media information. QA-SIVAS scores ranged from 9 to 14 out of 18; no study satisfied every video-quality requirement, only one included a noninjured control group, and none of the three quantitative biomechanical studies used a validated measurement method. Video-based identification can miss injuries that occur off camera, are obscured, or do not have a visually detectable event, creating selection and ascertainment limits. None of the included studies satisfied the QA-SIVAS requirement for validated parallax correction or motion quantification, and the general absence of control observations prevents causal conclusions about the observed movements. The literature showed substantial methodological, taxonomic, and operational heterogeneity; the review's proposed synthesis is descriptive and has not yet been validated as a guideline, checklist, or standardized framework.
paper.limitations: The review was limited to English-language studies, had restricted gray-literature coverage, and was dominated by male professional soccer. The authors caution that results may not transfer to youth, female, or nonprofessional populations; the search was last updated on 12 December 2024. The included studies were heterogeneous and frequently lacked validated kinematic methods, controls, diagnostic confirmation, and reliability assessment. Applicability to collegiate American football is indirect because the sport, movement demands, contact environment, and injury-documentation systems differ.
paper.practicalImplications: Video review can support structured description and hypothesis generation after a hamstring injury, but it should not be treated as a stand-alone causal test. Programs should clinically verify the diagnosis, define the injury frame and allowable timing uncertainty, use multiple blinded raters where possible, report camera views and frame rate, and distinguish visible observations from biomechanical estimates. The paper supports improving review procedures in soccer; it does not validate a specific screening or prevention rule for American football.
